before.description:
In 1386, a pig was dressed in a man's clothes and executed after a real court trial. It wasn't a joke — for centuries, European courts put animals on trial.

Pigs, bulls, rats, a rooster and even weevils got summonses, lawyers and verdicts. We follow the Pig of Falaise, the lawyer who defended rats (and blamed the cats), the rooster burned for laying an egg, and the weevils who were offered their own land — then reveal the surprising reason church courts kept holding these trials.

Chapters
0:00 The pig in the square
0:48 The Pig of Falaise
1:44 Two kinds of court
2:23 The lawyer for the rats
3:25 The rooster of Basel
4:13 The weevils' land deal
5:24 The real why
6:19 The end of animal trials

Sources

before.description:
Imagine being paid to swallow a toad, eat a dead man's sins, or empty toilets by hand at night. These were real jobs in old England.

We rank eight of the worst jobs in English history, from the ale conner who tasted every brewer's ale, to the Groom of the Stool who helped the king on the toilet, the toad eater, the sin eater, the saltpetre man who could dig up your floor, the fuller stamping cloth in stale urine, the tanner, and the gong farmer — with the real records behind each one.

before.description:
Steel wasn't invented on purpose. Ancient smiths heated soft iron in charcoal for hours, a little carbon soaked in, and the metal came out harder and sharper.

The oldest known steel was found at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey and dates to about 1800 BC. Smiths in southern India later made famous wootz steel.

Sources:

- World History Encyclopedia: Twelve Steels That Forged History
- Ferrous metallurgy overview (carburization, wootz steel)

tags: what happens if you step in quicksand
before.description:
Movies lied to you about quicksand. It can't swallow you whole: it's about twice as dense as your body, so you float and stop at about your waist. But it grips your legs hard, so here's how to get out, and the real danger nobody mentions.

Would you stay calm?

Sources: Khaldoun et al., "Liquefaction of quicksand under stress", Nature 437, 635 (2005); National Geographic, "Quicksand Science"; Live Science, "Quicksand Myth Debunked"; Europhysics News 37/4 (2006).

before.description:
Something ice cold hits the roof of your mouth, a big blood vessel feeding your brain suddenly widens, and the pressure inside your skull rises. The twist: the nerve that reports that pain also covers your forehead, so your brain blames your forehead. Press your tongue to the roof of your mouth or sip something warm and it fades in seconds.

Does it get you too?

Sources: Serrador et al., presentation at Experimental Biology 2012 (reported by ScienceDaily and the American Physiological Society); Cleveland Clinic, "Brain Freeze (Ice Cream Headache)"; NBC News, "Brain freeze: why ice cream makes some scream".
For curiosity only, not medical advice.

before.description:
Try to tickle yourself: nothing happens. Your brain predicts exactly what your own fingers will feel and turns the feeling down. Scientists proved it with a tickle robot: add a delay of just a fifth of a second and the tickle comes back.

Are you ticklish?

before.description:
In 1954, two Comet jets, the world's first jet airliners, broke apart in the air within months. To find out why, engineers sank a whole Comet in a giant water tank and pumped it up and down like thousands of flights, until a crack appeared at the sharp corner of a squarish window. Stress piles up at sharp corners. Round corners spread it out, so every airliner window since has rounded corners.

What other shapes around you are hiding a reason?

Sources: FAA Lessons Learned, "de Havilland DH-106 Comet 1"; Aviation Safety Network (Comet G-ALYP, 1954); This Day in Aviation, "Metal Fatigue"; Plane & Pilot magazine.
Animation, music and sound: TrueWhys (original). Fonts: Lilita One (Open Font License).

before.description:
Castle toilets were called garderobes: tiny rooms on the outer wall with a stone seat, and a chute that dropped straight down the outside of the wall, often into the moat. In 1204, French soldiers were besieging Château Gaillard, one of the strongest castles in Europe. Accounts say a few men climbed up a latrine chute, got inside and let their army in. Later castles added bars and bends to their chutes.

Would you have climbed it?

Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Toilets in a Medieval Castle"; Siege of Château Gaillard (1203–1204), overview of the accounts; Kaufmann & Kaufmann, The Medieval Fortress. Details of the climb differ between accounts.
Animation, music and sound: TrueWhys (original). Fonts: Lilita One (Open Font License).

tags: can you open a plane door mid flight
before.description:
What happens if someone pulls the door handle at 35,000 feet? Nothing. The cabin is pumped full of air, much thicker than the thin air outside, and that air pushes on every part of the plane, including the door. On most jets the door is a plug: bigger than its frame, so it has to move inward before it can swing out. The air presses it into the frame with about eight tonnes of force, more than a big elephant.

So next time you sit by the exit... relax.

Sources: Patrick Smith, Ask the Pilot, "Open Door Policy"; AirlineRatings, "Can you open an aircraft door mid flight?"; FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (pressurisation). The eight-tonne figure is our estimate from a cabin pressure difference of about 8 psi on a door of about 1.5 square metres.
Animation, music and sound: TrueWhys (original). Fonts: Lilita One (Open Font License).

tags: why you should never eat polar bear liver
before.description:
Over 400 years ago, Dutch sailors stuck in the Arctic cooked a polar bear's liver. Days later they fell sick and their skin began to peel. The reason: vitamin A. It piles up the food chain, from fish to seals to bears, and just one gram of polar bear liver holds more than an adult's limit for a whole day.

Would you have known?

Sources: Gerrit de Veer's journal of Barents' third voyage (1597); Rodahl & Moore, "The vitamin A content and toxicity of bear and seal liver", Biochemical Journal 37, 166 (1943); NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin A fact sheet; Rodahl, Norsk Polarinstitutt Skrifter 95 (1949).
Animation and music: TrueWhys (original).
TrueWhys — the real story behind life's weirdest whys.
